summary:
Kemerovo Oblast stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, and that framework is assessed in full here. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023; the Supreme Court designated the "international LGBT movement" extremist in November 2023; and the expanded propaganda statute punishes any public expression promoting non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition, expressly including material that justifies transition. Consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and the constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people, according to the UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression for Russia (June 2025).

The penalties a visitor would face are administrative at first instance and criminal on repetition. Fines run to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or up to 15 days' detention, with repeat offences risking criminal prosecution. The US State Department advisory adds that a foreigner found guilty under the propaganda law may be arrested, detained for up to 15 days and deported, and states that displaying certain symbols, including the rainbow flag, is a crime. That advisory advises against all travel to Russia regardless of personal characteristics.

One enforcement action is documented within Kemerovo Oblast itself. A person already serving a prison sentence there received an additional six-year sentence in February for participating in the "LGBT movement" and for "involving" other prisoners in its activities, RIA Novosti reported, citing the Federal Security Service. No other unit-specific finding appears in the sources: all three are national in scope, and the UK Home Office note contains no division-specific information beyond the national framework, so this oblast inherits the national position with a single corroborating incident.

The national enforcement volume behind that position is documented. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for participating in the designated movement or displaying its symbols since the November 2023 designation, with sentences of up to 12 years in prison, as of 30 June 2025. It also documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols, mostly on social media, and 257 "gay propaganda" penalties imposed in 2023-24 against 22 in 2021-22.
tangentialFactors:
The trajectory of enforcement is upward on every measured axis. Propaganda penalties rose from 22 in 2021-22 to 257 in 2023-24, a factor of roughly eleven, while the post-designation extremism docket produced 101 convictions carrying sentences as long as 12 years within eighteen months of the Supreme Court's ruling.

The designation operates alongside pre-existing coercion rather than replacing it. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) reported the case of "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping after police responded to a phone she had found. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical raids followed the designation within days. The Guardian reported on 17 January 2024 that within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, ordering about 100 patrons at one venue to face walls for search and photograph, with at least two other venues raided the same night. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two years preceding.

The regime places Russia among the most hostile jurisdictions covered by this map, and several foreign governments treat it as such: the US State Department rates travel to Russia Level 4, Do Not Travel, with warnings addressed specifically to LGBT travellers.
localsOnly:
Residents of Kemerovo Oblast face the same statutes as visitors, but with the residency exposure that visitors can escape by leaving. Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals across Russia were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement, according to the UK Home Office country policy and information note (June 2025).

Symbol display is the most common charge locally and nationally. Human Rights Watch documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 under article 20.3 of the administrative code for displaying banned symbols, most of them on social media, alongside the 101 extremism convictions carrying up to 12 years.

The Kemerovo incident indicates that the extremism designation reaches inside the penal system: the additional six-year term was imposed on a prisoner already serving time, for alleged activity involving other inmates, and the report came through RIA Novosti citing the Federal Security Service rather than through a court press service.

LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, are recognised as a particular social group under the refugee convention by the UK Home Office, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.
outOfScopeNotes:
The UK Home Office country policy and information note (June 2025) contains no division-specific information on Kemerovo Oblast beyond the national framework; the absence of further local findings in these three national sources is unresolved rather than evidence that no further incidents occurred.

The date of the Kemerovo sentence is given only as "February" in the source, without a year; it appears in a report published 30 June 2025 but the exact month-year is not sourced here.

Whether oblast-level bodies in Kemerovo Oblast have conducted raids, inspections or campaigns of their own is not addressed by any source in this inventory.

The relationship between the six-year sentence's stated basis, participation in the movement and "involving" other prisoners, and the evidentiary standard applied is not examined in the available material.
